title: Particles: one picture that explains why solids hold, liquids pour and gases squash

summary.text: One drop of red food colour turns a cup of water pink. Pour a spoonful of that pink water into fresh water, and then again, and again, and the colour fades but does not stop at once. Press the plunger of a syringe full of air, and it squashes to less than half. Press one full of water, and it will not move. Your child dilutes colour through a row of cups and squeezes air, water and rice. Then they build one picture, the particle model, that explains what a solid, a liquid and a gas are, and why the air in a pressure cooker can make it whistle.
summary.art: A row of six clear cups on a white paper, the water going from deep pink on the left to almost clear on the right, with a syringe of air and a syringe of water beside them.

intro.hook: Put one drop of red colour into a cup of water, and the whole cup turns pink. Now take a spoonful of that pink water and mix it into a fresh cup. Do it again, and again. How many cups can one single drop colour before the pink is gone?
intro.text: The answer is surprising, and it tells us something big. A drop is made of far more tiny pieces than anyone can count, and those pieces spread into every cup. In this unit you test how far one drop goes, and you squeeze air, water and rice in a syringe. You find out why air squashes and water does not, and why a steel spoon holds its shape while the steam in a cooker pushes on the lid. One picture explains all of it: everything is made of particles, and what a solid, a liquid and a gas do depends on how close the particles are and how they move.
intro.art: A child at a kitchen table with a row of cups of fading pink water, a teaspoon and a small bottle of red food colour.

outcomes: I can say the difference between a material, a substance and a mixture, and give an example of each.
I can describe how particles are arranged and how they move in a solid, a liquid and a gas, and draw each one.
I can use the particle model to explain why a solid keeps its shape, a liquid pours and a gas spreads out to fill a space.
I can show with a dilution test that a tiny drop holds a huge number of particles, and that colour I cannot see can still be there.
I can explain with a syringe test why air can be squashed but water and solids hardly can, using the idea of empty space between particles.
I can explain that gas pressure comes from particles hitting the walls, and why heating a sealed gas makes the push bigger.
I can say what a model is, give one thing the particle model explains well and one thing it gets wrong.
I can tell how the idea that gas particles fly about was ignored for a hundred years, and what changed minds.

terms.meaning: A material is what an object is made of. Many different objects can be made of the same material.
terms.example: A katori and a ladle can both be made of steel. A spoon can be made of wood.
terms.art: A steel katori, a steel ladle and a wooden spoon on a kitchen shelf, with the word steel under the first two.

terms.meaning: A substance is one particular kind of stuff. All of it is made of the same kind of particle.
terms.example: Water, salt, sugar and iron are substances.
terms.art: Four small jars labelled water, salt, sugar and iron nails.

terms.meaning: A mixture is two or more substances mixed together, with each keeping its own particles. You can often separate them again.
terms.example: Air, sambar and sugar water are mixtures.
terms.art: A bowl of sambar with dal, vegetables and water, and a label that says mixture.

terms.meaning: A particle is a very tiny piece that a substance is made of. It is far too small to see, even with a magnifying glass.
terms.example: A drop of water holds more than a thousand million million million water particles.
terms.art: A drop of water on a finger, with a circle zooming in to show many small blue dots.

terms.meaning: An atom is one of the tiny building blocks that everything is made of. There are about a hundred different kinds.
terms.example: Iron is made of iron atoms. Water has hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms.
terms.art: A cluster of round dots of different colours labelled hydrogen, oxygen, carbon and iron.

terms.meaning: A molecule is a small group of atoms joined together. Many substances are made of molecules.
terms.example: A water molecule has three atoms joined: two of hydrogen and one of oxygen.
terms.art: A water molecule drawn as one large red ball with two small white balls joined to it.

terms.meaning: The state of a substance is whether it is a solid, a liquid or a gas. The state depends on how its particles are arranged and moving.
terms.example: Ice, water and steam are three states of the same substance.
terms.art: Three small pictures of the same water: an ice cube, a glass of water and steam rising from a kettle.

terms.meaning: A solid keeps its own shape and its own size. Its particles are close together and held in place.
terms.example: A steel spoon stays a spoon shape in a drawer or in a cup.
terms.art: A steel spoon with a zoomed-in circle showing particles in neat rows.

terms.meaning: A liquid keeps its size but takes the shape of its container. Its particles are close together but slide past each other.
terms.example: Water takes the shape of a tumbler, then the shape of a bowl.
terms.art: Water in a tumbler and in a bowl, with a zoomed-in circle showing close, jumbled particles.

terms.meaning: A gas has no shape or size of its own. It spreads to fill the whole space it is in. Its particles are far apart and fly about.
terms.example: The steam in a kettle fills the kettle. The smell of cooking fills the house.
terms.art: A balloon with a zoomed-in circle showing a few particles far apart with arrows.

terms.meaning: To compress something is to squeeze it into a smaller space.
terms.example: You can compress the air in a bicycle pump. You cannot compress the water in a bottle.
terms.art: A hand pressing the plunger of a bicycle pump.

terms.meaning: Gas pressure is the push that a gas makes on the walls of its container. It comes from particles hitting the walls.
terms.example: The air inside a football pushes outwards on the leather and keeps it round.
terms.art: A football cut open, with arrows from air particles hitting the inside of the wall.

terms.meaning: Diffusion is the slow spreading of particles through a gas or a liquid, just by their own movement, with no stirring.
terms.example: The smell of an agarbatti slowly reaches the far corner of the room.
terms.art: A stick of agarbatti with smell dots spreading across a room.

terms.meaning: To dilute a coloured or strong liquid is to add more water, so there is less of the strong stuff in each spoonful.
terms.example: Adding water to a thick squash makes it weaker and paler.
terms.art: A glass of dark squash being topped up with water until it is pale.

terms.meaning: A gap is the empty space between particles. Nothing at all is in it.
terms.example: The gaps between air particles are why air can be squashed.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle with a few particles and the gaps between them marked with arrows.

terms.meaning: A model is a picture, drawing or object that helps us think about something we cannot see. A model is useful, but it is never exactly the real thing.
terms.example: A tray of rice can be a model of particles in a solid, a liquid or a gas.
terms.art: A tray of rice grains next to a drawing of particles.

terms.meaning: Evidence is something you see, measure or find out that shows an idea is right or wrong.
terms.example: The air in a syringe squashed to half, and that is evidence that there is space between air particles.
terms.art: A child writing numbers in a notebook next to a syringe.

explanations.definition: A material is what an object is made of. A substance is one kind of stuff, made of one kind of particle. A mixture has two or more substances.
explanations.description: Steel is a material. Salt is a substance, because every salt particle is the same. Air is a mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen with about one fifth oxygen and small amounts of other gases. Sambar is a mixture of water, dal, tamarind and spices. In a mixture, the substances keep their own particles, and often you can get them apart again. In a substance, you cannot get it apart by simple means such as sieving or letting it settle.
examples: Sea water is a mixture of water and salt. The salt can be got back by letting the water dry in the sun.
Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc, melted together.
Distilled water, which is used in car batteries, is very nearly a pure substance.
explanations.art: A table with three groups: steel spoon labelled material, salt labelled substance, and sambar labelled mixture.
explanations.context: This card says what material, substance and mixture mean, because the rest of the unit uses these words.

explanations.concept: Solids: particles packed close and held in place
explanations.definition: In a solid, the particles touch their neighbours and are held in place by pulls between them. They jiggle on the spot, but they do not move around.
explanations.description: The pulls between particles are strong in a solid. Each particle is held by its neighbours, like a person in a tightly packed row of seats. The particles can shake a little, but they cannot swap places. That is why a solid keeps its shape and its size. In many solids, such as salt and ice, the particles sit in neat repeating rows. Heating a solid makes the particles shake harder.
examples: A steel katori keeps its shape when you carry it from the shelf to the table.
An ice cube keeps its shape until it warms up.
Rock salt grains have flat faces because their particles are stacked in neat rows.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle with particles in neat rows, each with small curved marks to show it jiggling on the spot.
explanations.context: This card describes the particles in a solid.

explanations.concept: Liquids: particles close together but sliding
explanations.definition: In a liquid, the particles touch their neighbours but are not held in place. They slide past each other all the time.
explanations.description: The particles in a liquid are about as close as in a solid, but the pulls between them are weaker. They move around and swap places. That is why a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. The particles still touch, so a liquid keeps its size. Pour a litre of water into any shape of jug, and it is still a litre.
examples: Water poured from a bottle into a tumbler takes the shape of the tumbler.
A cup of milk is still a cup of milk if you pour it into a wide plate.
Honey slides slowly because its particles stick to each other more.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle with particles close together in a jumbled pile, with arrows showing them sliding.
explanations.context: This card describes the particles in a liquid.

explanations.concept: Gases: particles far apart and flying
explanations.definition: In a gas, the particles are very far apart compared with their size. They fly about in straight lines until they hit something.
explanations.description: Gas particles hardly pull on each other at all. Each one flies in a straight line until it bumps into another particle or a wall, and then it bounces off. In air at room temperature, the particles travel about five hundred metres every second. That is faster than the speed of sound, which is about 340 metres a second. A gas has no size of its own, so it spreads out into every corner of whatever holds it. Between the particles there is only empty space.
examples: The steam from a kettle spreads out until you cannot see it.
The smell of tadka spreads from the kitchen to the bedroom.
A balloon is round because gas particles push on its skin from the inside, in all directions.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle with a few particles far apart, each with a long arrow showing how fast it flies.
explanations.context: This card describes the particles in a gas.

explanations.definition: Between the particles of every substance there is empty space. In a gas there is a lot of it. In a liquid or a solid there is much less.
explanations.description: When you squeeze air in a syringe, it squashes to half, because the particles move closer together into the empty space. A liquid or a solid cannot be squeezed much, because their particles are already touching. The same idea explains something odd. Pour 100 millilitres of fine mustard seeds into 100 millilitres of big chana dal, and the total is much less than 200. The small seeds fall into the gaps between the big dal. Particles of different sizes fit into each other's gaps in the same way.
examples: Salt dissolved in a full glass of water hardly changes the level, because the salt particles fit between the water particles.
A balloon full of air can be squeezed smaller, but a balloon full of water cannot.
Bicycle tyres can be pumped up, because more and more air particles can be pushed into the same space.
explanations.art: Two syringes side by side: one with air showing the plunger pushed in halfway, one with water showing the plunger stuck.
explanations.context: This card explains why gases can be squashed and liquids cannot, using empty space.

explanations.definition: A solid, a liquid and a gas can be made of exactly the same particles. Ice, water and steam are all water. What changes is how fast the particles move and how strongly they hold each other.
explanations.description: Heat a solid, and its particles shake harder. At some warmth they break out of their places, and the solid melts into a liquid. Heat the liquid more, and the fastest particles escape and fly off as a gas. Nothing new is made. The water particles in steam are the same as in ice. Each is a molecule of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Cool the steam on a cold steel plate, and the particles slow down and cling together as drops of water again.
examples: A candle's wax melts and runs, and it is still wax when it sets.
Steam on a cold plate turns back to water drops.
Ghee melts in a pan and sets again as it cools.
explanations.art: Three pictures of the same water: ice with particles in rows, water with particles jumbled and close, and steam with particles far apart.
explanations.context: This card explains that the three states are not three different stuffs.

explanations.concept: Gas pressure: the push of particles on walls
explanations.definition: Gas pressure is the push of a gas on a surface. It is made by countless particles hitting the surface and bouncing off.
explanations.description: One particle hitting a wall makes a push far too small to feel. But in a football there are so many particles, hitting so often, that together the push is steady and strong. The air outside pushes on you with about the weight of a one-kilogram bag on every square centimetre. You do not notice it, because the same push is inside your body too. If you heat a gas in a sealed container, its particles move faster, hit the walls harder and more often, and the pressure goes up. A pressure cooker uses this. The sealed steam pushes at about twice the pressure of the outside air.
examples: A bicycle tyre is hard because the air inside pushes outwards at about three times the push of the outside air.
A balloon left in a hot car can burst, because the hot air inside pushes harder.
A cooker's whistle lifts when the steam inside pushes up on the weight.
explanations.art: A pressure cooker cut in half, with steam particles shown hitting the lid and walls with arrows.
explanations.context: This card explains why a gas pushes on its container.

explanations.concept: Why smells take minutes, not seconds
explanations.definition: Gas particles fly very fast, but they bump into other air particles billions of times every second. So a smell wanders slowly across a room, spreading by diffusion.
explanations.description: A smell particle leaving an agarbatti is moving at hundreds of metres a second. But it travels less than a ten-thousandth of a millimetre before it collides with an air particle and is knocked in a new direction. It zigzags. After billions of knocks, it has gone only a little way from where it began. Moving air from a fan or an open window carries it far faster than diffusion alone. In a liquid, particles are even closer, so diffusion is far slower still, which is why colour in unstirred water takes hours.
examples: A smell reaches the next room mostly because air currents carry it.
Colour in unstirred water takes hours to spread through a glass.
Warm air spreads smells faster, because its particles move faster.
explanations.art: A zigzag line showing one smell particle bouncing between many air particles on its way across a room.
explanations.context: This card explains why a smell takes minutes to cross a room, though gas particles are very fast.

explanations.concept: How many particles are in a drop?
explanations.definition: A drop of water holds more than a thousand million million million water particles. That is a 1 followed by 21 zeros. A drop of food colour holds a huge number of colour particles too.
explanations.description: A water particle, one molecule, is about three ten-millionths of a millimetre across. Such sizes are almost impossible to imagine. So scientists use comparisons. If every person alive today counted one particle each second, it would take them more than six thousand years to count the particles in one drop of water. This is why one drop of colour can colour a whole cup and can still be there, in tiny amounts, in a cup that looks clear. A tiny share of a huge number is still a huge number.
examples: Even the faintest pink cup still holds millions of colour particles in each teaspoon.
A teaspoon of sea water holds many millions of millions of salt particles.
A single breath holds more air particles than there are grains of sand in all the beaches on Earth, by some estimates.
explanations.art: A drop of water on a fingertip, with arrows pointing to a long number of zeros.
explanations.context: This card explains how many particles one drop holds.

explanations.concept: Inside a particle: atoms are mostly empty space
explanations.definition: Every particle is made of one or more atoms, and an atom is mostly empty space. The middle of the atom, the nucleus, is about a hundred thousand times smaller than the whole atom.
explanations.description: Imagine an atom the size of a big cricket ground. The nucleus in the middle would be about the size of a mustard seed. Around it, tiny particles called electrons zip about. So why does a table feel solid, if its atoms are nearly empty? The electrons of the atoms in your hand push on the electrons of the atoms in the table. This electric push is strong, and it stops them getting closer. What we feel as hardness is this push between atoms.
examples: A water molecule has three atoms: two of hydrogen and one of oxygen.
A sugar molecule has 45 atoms.
A hammer feels hard because the atoms in it push strongly on each other.
explanations.art: An atom drawn as a big cricket ground with a mustard seed in the middle and tiny dots far away at the edge.
explanations.context: This card goes deeper and looks inside the particles.

explanations.concept: Grains and powders: a solid that flows
explanations.definition: A heap of rice or sand can pour like a liquid, but each grain is a solid. The particles of a substance are far smaller than the grains.
explanations.description: When you pour rice, the heap flows and takes the shape of the bowl. This makes it look like a liquid. But each grain keeps its own shape, and there is air between the grains. The grains are solid because the tiny particles inside each grain are locked in place. Pouring rice is a nice picture of a liquid, but it is not what a liquid is. A tray of rice is a useful model, but it is not an exact one.
examples: Sand runs through an hourglass like a liquid.
Atta pours from a tin but a lump of atta dough does not.
A sack of cement powder spills across the floor, but each tiny grain is a solid.
explanations.art: A heap of rice on a plate, with a zoomed-in circle on one grain showing neat rows of particles.
explanations.context: This card warns that a heap of solid grains is not the same as a liquid.

explanations.concept: A model: useful, and always a little wrong
explanations.description: The particle model is a picture that explains a lot: why things have states, why gases squash, why smells spread. But no model is exactly right. We draw particles as tiny balls, yet real atoms are fuzzy and have no sharp edge. Physicists now describe the smallest things as ripples in fields, not as tiny balls. Even so, the particle model gives correct answers to most questions about solids, liquids and gases, which is why scientists use it. A good scientist keeps asking where a model stops working.
examples: A drawing of a particle as a ball is a model.
A tray of rice shaken to show a gas is a model.
Scientists use computer models of particles to design new materials.
explanations.art: A ball-and-stick drawing of a molecule next to a fuzzy cloud drawing of the same molecule.
explanations.context: This card is about what a model is, and why we should check where it stops working.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree that everything is made of particles.
agreed.text: Everything is made of particles too small to see, and the three states differ in how the particles are arranged and move.
agreed.evidence: The model predicts how gases squash, how they push, how fast smells spread and how solids melt, and the measurements match.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree about the empty space in a gas.
agreed.text: In a gas, the particles are far apart with empty space between them. That is why gases can be squashed.
agreed.evidence: Air squashes to a fraction of its size under pressure, and the pressure and volume follow a regular rule that the particle model predicts.

agreed.context: This card is about gas pressure.
agreed.text: Gas pressure is made by particles hitting the walls, and a hotter gas pushes harder.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of gases at different warmths match the numbers worked out from fast-moving particles.

agreed.context: This card is about the states of one substance.
agreed.text: Ice, water and steam are the same substance, and only the arrangement and motion of the particles differ.
agreed.evidence: Weighing before and after melting or boiling in closed containers gives the same mass, and cooling steam gives back water.

agreed.text: Atoms are mostly empty space, with a tiny nucleus in the middle.
agreed.evidence: In the early 1900s, experiments aimed fast particles at thin gold foil, and nearly all went straight through.

agreed.context: This card is about what particles do in a solid.
agreed.text: Particles in a solid are never still. They jiggle on the spot, more as the solid is warmed.
agreed.evidence: Heat makes solids expand, and X-ray and neutron measurements show the jiggle of the particles.

challenging.context: This card is about a very common picture.
challenging.claim: Particles are tiny hard balls with a clear edge.
challenging.who: Most school drawings and many textbooks
challenging.for: Balls explain how particles pack together and slide past each other.
challenging.against: Real atoms have no sharp edge. They are better described as fuzzy clouds, and physicists now describe the smallest parts as ripples in fields. Balls are a useful picture but not the truth.

challenging.context: This card is about the air in the room.
challenging.claim: Air is nothing. A room with no furniture is empty.
challenging.who: Many young children, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: You cannot see air, and you can walk through it easily.
challenging.against: A balloon blown up with air weighs a little more than an empty one. Air squashes in a syringe, pushes on a tyre and carries sound. It is real stuff, with particles far apart.

challenging.context: This card is about the space between particles.
challenging.claim: Between the particles of air there is more air, or dust, or tiny invisible stuff.
challenging.for: It is hard to imagine nothing at all.
challenging.against: If something filled the gaps, air could not be squashed, because there would be nothing for the particles to move into. The rule for how the volume of a gas changes with pressure only works if the gaps between the particles are empty.

challenging.claim: When a substance is heated, its particles get bigger.
challenging.for: Things expand when heated, so the particles must grow.
challenging.against: The particles stay the same size. They move faster and push each other further apart, so the whole thing takes up more room.

challenging.context: This card is about gases and a history of the idea.
challenging.claim: Gas particles sit in fixed places and push each other away, like people in a crowd holding out their arms.
challenging.who: Many scientists in the 1700s, following Isaac Newton's maths
challenging.for: This picture also gives the right rule for how gas volume changes with pressure.
challenging.against: It cannot explain why a hot gas pushes harder, or why gases spread into each other. In 1738, Daniel Bernoulli showed that fast-flying particles explain all of these.

challenging.claim: The particles in a solid do not move at all.
challenging.for: A solid does not seem to move.
challenging.against: The particles jiggle on the spot. Warm a solid and they jiggle more, until the solid melts. Solids that look still are full of movement.

challenging.context: This card is about liquids and heat.
challenging.claim: A liquid cannot be squeezed at all, not even a tiny bit.
challenging.who: Many textbooks and many scientists before the 1760s
challenging.for: In a syringe, water seems not to move, no matter how hard you press.
challenging.against: Very careful experiments show water can be squeezed a very small amount, less than one part in ten thousand for each extra push of one atmosphere. The particles are touching but not perfectly rigid.

big_questions.q: A drop of colour made a whole cup pink, and was still there in a cup that looked clear. How would you prove that something is in the water if you cannot see it?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tests that could find it with something other than your eyes. Taste is one. What other senses could you use?

big_questions.q: Air squashes and water does not. Both are made of particles. So what must be different about them?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when you try to push particles closer together. What stops them?

big_questions.q: If an atom is mostly empty space, why can't you push your hand through a wall?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the atoms in your hand and the atoms in the wall do when they come close.

big_questions.q: A steel spoon, a cup of water and the steam of a kettle can be the same particles. Is the spoon a different thing from the steam?
big_questions.hint: Think about ice, water and steam. What is the same, and what is different?

big_questions.q: Nobody has ever seen a gas particle with their eyes. How can we be sure that they are there?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you tested in this unit, and what it would mean if there were no particles.

big_questions.q: A model is a picture that is not exactly true but is very useful. Can you think of other models in life, such as a map?
big_questions.hint: A map shows roads but not every tree. What does it leave out? What would be lost if it showed everything?

big_questions.q: The air in a room is made of particles flying at five hundred metres a second, and we feel nothing. Why not?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many particles hit you every second, and whether they push from only one side.

big_questions.q: Scientists once ignored the idea of flying gas particles for a hundred years. Why might a good idea be ignored for so long?
big_questions.hint: Think about who proposed it, who read it, and what evidence people thought they had.

big_questions.q: If you could keep pushing air into a syringe until its particles touched, what would it become?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a gas is like when its particles are very close together, as in a liquid. Very strong squeezing and cooling can do this.

story.title: The Cooker That Did Not Whistle
story.note: A made-up story. Lalitha, her Paati and her uncle are imagined. The science is real. A pressure cooker has a weight on a vent that lifts and whistles when the steam pushes hard enough, and a lid that will not open while there is pressure inside. Always let a cooker cool, and never force the lid.
text: On Sundays in Mysuru, the whole family sat down to lunch at one o'clock. This Sunday, Lalitha's Paati had to go to the temple early. She gave Lalitha a big job.
'The dal and rice are in the cooker,' said Paati. 'Put it on the flame. Count the whistles. After three whistles, turn off the gas. Do not touch anything else. I will be back before it is ready.'
Lalitha was ten, and she had counted whistles many times. She lit the stove and sat on a stool, with her chin on her hands. The kitchen smelled of jasmine from the pooja shelf and of fresh coffee.
In a few minutes the cooker began to hiss. The steel weight on top rattled. Pssshh! The first whistle. Lalitha smiled and held up one finger. Pssshh! The second. She held up two.
Then she waited for the third. And she waited.

Nothing came. The cooker was still hissing, but the weight on the top was not moving at all. Lalitha stood up and looked closer. A thin silver thread of steam was slipping out from the side of the lid, with a high thin sound, like a kettle far away.

Her uncle Raghu walked in. He was a big, cheerful man, and he had come from Bengaluru for lunch. He was also very hungry. 'Ah, the cooker,' he said. 'Is lunch ready? Let me open it and look.' He reached for the lid handle with a kitchen cloth.
'Please don't, Mama,' said Lalitha. 'Turn the lid and see. It will not move.'
He tried. He pulled and twisted. The lid did not move. 'Stuck,' said Raghu. 'These old cookers. Give me a spoon, I will force it. Or I will put the whole thing under the tap.'

Lalitha switched off the gas. Then she did something she was proud of for a long time. She stood very still, and she thought about the cooker the way her teacher had taught her to think about everything. She pictured the steam as a crowd of tiny particles, too small to see, flying about at hundreds of metres a second.

'Mama, listen,' she said. 'Inside there is water, and the flame heated it until a lot of it turned into steam. Steam is a gas. Its particles fly in all directions and hit the walls and the lid. The lid is shut, so they have nowhere to go. They are pushing on the lid right now, much harder than the air outside pushes. That is why it will not open.'
Raghu's hand stopped on the handle. 'And the whistle?'

'The weight is supposed to lift when the push gets big enough,' said Lalitha. 'Then steam escapes, and that is the whistle. This one did not lift. Something is blocking the little pipe under it. So the push has built up, and the steam is finding a way out at the side. If you force the lid, the steam will come out all at once.'
Raghu took his hand off the lid. He stepped back, and so did Lalitha. They stood by the door, and they waited.

Five minutes passed. The hiss grew softer. 'The flame is off,' said Lalitha, 'so the steam cools. Its particles slow down. They hit the lid less hard and less often. When the push inside is the same as the push outside, the lid will open easily.'

After fifteen minutes the hiss had stopped. Lalitha put a hand near the lid, not on it. It was only warm. 'Now,' she said. Raghu turned the handle. The lid slid open with a soft sigh, and a cloud of steam rose and spread and was gone.

The dal was perfectly cooked. Lalitha lifted the weight and looked into the little pipe with a torch. A tiny skin of dal had dried inside it, like a plug. She cleaned it with a toothpick while her uncle held the torch.

When Paati came back from the temple, Raghu told her everything. 'Your granddaughter stopped me from opening a cooker full of steam,' he said. 'She explained it better than my physics teacher ever did.'

Paati looked at the pipe, at the toothpick, and at Lalitha. 'Next time,' she said, 'we will clean the pipe before we start. But I am glad you counted the whistles, and glad you noticed when the third did not come.'
That afternoon, over the best dal he had ever eaten, Raghu asked Lalitha to explain it all again, from the beginning.
story.epiphany: Steam is a gas, made of fast-flying particles. In a sealed cooker they hit the walls and the lid, and that push is pressure. Cooling slows the particles, so the push falls and the lid opens.
ask: Why would the lid not open while the cooker was hot and sealed?
Why did Lalitha switch off the flame and wait, instead of opening the cooker?
What happens to the steam particles as the cooker cools, and why does that help the lid open?
How could Lalitha tell that the weight was not lifting, and what did she think was wrong?
Lalitha explained a cooker to her uncle by picturing particles. Why is a picture of invisible particles useful here?
