games.title: Which Crowd? A card game about particles
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something that happens at home. You decide if it is a solid, a liquid, a gas or a change, and you explain it with particle words.

setup.art: A table with a sheet of paper divided into four columns labelled Solid, Liquid, Gas and Changing, and a pile of cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a mat with four columns. Cut out the cards and the word tokens.

setup.art: A child reading the front of a card aloud while another child holds two word tokens.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it in a column. Pick two word tokens to explain it.

setup.art: A card turned over to show its answer, with the two correct word tokens beside it and a hand adding a point on a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. Score your points.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a thing that happens at home on the front, and the answer with the right word tokens on the back

items.f: A steel katori falls on the floor and keeps its shape.
items.b: Solid. Tokens: Close together, Held in place.

items.f: Water from a jug takes the shape of the tumbler.
items.b: Liquid. Tokens: Close together, Slide past each other.

items.f: The smell of tadka reaches the bedroom.
items.b: Gas. Tokens: Far apart, Fly about. Moving air carries the smell too.

items.f: Ghee is runny in a hot pan and firm when it comes out of the fridge.
items.b: Changing. The same ghee is a solid when cool and a liquid when warm, as its particles jiggle harder. Tokens: Jiggle on the spot, Slide past each other.

items.f: You push the plunger of a syringe full of air, and it goes in half way.
items.b: Gas. Tokens: Far apart, Empty space between.

items.f: You push the plunger of a syringe full of water, and it hardly moves.
items.b: Liquid. Tokens: Close together, Slide past each other.

items.f: An ice cube sits on a plate in the sun and slowly turns to water.
items.b: Changing. The particles jiggle harder until they break out of their places. Tokens: Jiggle on the spot, Held in place.

items.f: A kettle's steam is invisible right at the spout.
items.b: Gas. Water vapour is a gas you cannot see. The white cloud further out is tiny drops of liquid water. Tokens: Far apart, Fly about.

items.f: Sand pours from your fist and heaps up on the floor.
items.b: Solid. It is many solid grains, and each grain has its particles held in place. Tokens: Close together, Held in place.

items.f: A balloon left in the sun gets tight.
items.b: Gas. The hotter air particles fly faster and hit the skin harder. Tokens: Fly about, Hit the walls.

items.f: Honey flows slowly from a jar.
items.b: Liquid. Tokens: Close together, Slide past each other.

items.f: A bicycle tyre feels hard.
items.b: Gas. Many air particles are squeezed in, and they hit the inside wall very often. Tokens: Fly about, Hit the walls.

items.f: The handle of a steel spoon gets warm when the bowl is in hot tea.
items.b: Solid. The jiggling passes from particle to particle along the spoon. Tokens: Jiggle on the spot, Held in place.

items.f: A camphor tablet in the open gets smaller, and you can smell it.
items.b: Changing. Particles leave the solid and fly into the air as a gas. Tokens: Fly about, Far apart.

items.f: A pump pushes air into a football.
items.b: Gas. More particles fit into the same space, so they hit the wall more often. Tokens: Hit the walls, Empty space between.

items.f: A drop of red colour spreads through a still glass of water over many hours.
items.b: Liquid. The particles are close, so they bump into each other a lot, and the spreading is slow. Tokens: Close together, Slide past each other.

items.f: A cup of water poured onto a wide plate is still a cup of water.
items.b: Liquid. The shape changes but the amount stays the same, because the particles are still touching. Tokens: Close together, Slide past each other.

items.f: Candle wax drips and then sets hard.
items.b: Changing. The wax particles slow down as they cool and become held in place. Tokens: Slide past each other, Held in place.

items.f: Wet clothes on the line are dry by evening.
items.b: Changing. Water particles escape from the liquid and fly off into the air. Tokens: Fly about, Far apart.

items.f: A steel ladle stays hard in boiling water.
items.b: Solid. The steel particles are held in place even when they jiggle faster. Tokens: Jiggle on the spot, Held in place.

items.f: The steam inside a closed cooker pushes on the lid.
items.b: Gas. Tokens: Fly about, Hit the walls.

items.f: A salt crystal has flat shiny faces.
items.b: Solid. The particles are stacked in neat rows. Tokens: Close together, Held in place.

items.f: Juice from a packet is poured into a glass.
items.b: Liquid. Tokens: Close together, Slide past each other.

items.f: You open a bottle of fizzy soda and hear a hiss.
items.b: Gas. Gas that was squeezed into the drink escapes into the air. Tokens: Far apart, Fly about.

printables.title: 8 word tokens: one word or short phrase on each

rules: Draw a mat on a sheet of paper with four columns: Solid, Liquid, Gas and Changing. Put the word tokens in a row where everyone can reach them.
Shuffle the 24 cards and make a pile with the fronts up. Take turns to be the player.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over. Put it in the column you think fits.
Pick the two word tokens that best explain your choice. Say one sentence that uses both words.
Now turn the card over and read the back. Right column: 1 point. Each of the two tokens that matches the back: 1 point more. A card can give up to 3 points.
If you were wrong, put the card in a Learn pile. Say what you would answer now.
Some cards say Changing, because the substance is changing from one state to another. For these, say what is speeding up or slowing down.
When all 24 cards are played, shuffle the Learn pile and play it once more. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone, try to get at least 48 points on the first round, and then beat your score with the Learn pile.

flow.do: 1. Draw the mat with four columns. 2. Cut out the cards and tokens. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, fronts up.
flow.say: This game is about particles. Each card is something that happens at home. You decide which column it goes in, and explain it with two word tokens.
flow.kid: Draw four columns. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Crowd? You set up the mat, the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. Read the steel katori card. Do not keep the points.
flow.say: Read the card. Which column does it go in? Pick two tokens that explain it. Then we check the back together.
flow.kid: Read the steel katori card. Pick a column. Pick two tokens. Check the back.
flow.parent: This practice card scores nothing. It shows the routine: column, two tokens, one sentence.

check.q: A steel katori falls on the floor and keeps its shape. Which column does it go in?
check.why: A steel katori keeps its shape, so it is a solid. Its particles are close together and held in place. Picking Liquid means thinking that a hard thing can flow. Picking Gas means forgetting that a gas has no shape of its own.

flow.do: Play the first twelve cards, taking turns. After each card, turn it over and give out the points. Put wrong cards in the Learn pile.
flow.say: Read the card, choose a column and two tokens, and say your sentence. Then turn the card over. Did you get the column? Did you get the tokens?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a column. Pick two tokens. Turn it over.

ask.q: What do the gas cards have in common?
good: The particles are far apart.
The particles fly about.
There is a lot of empty space between the particles.

flow.parent: Help your child use the word tokens in a full sentence, such as 'The particles are far apart, so the air can be squashed.'

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards. Add up the points. Then shuffle the Learn pile and play it once more.
flow.say: These are the last twelve cards. Count your points when they are done. Then we replay the cards you got wrong.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points. Replay the Learn pile.
flow.parent: Some cards can feel tricky, such as the sand card. Sand pours like a liquid, but each grain is a solid.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child think for a moment before they answer.
flow.say: Look at the Changing cards. What do ice, ghee, wax and camphor have in common?
flow.kid: Look at the Changing cards. What do they have in common?

ask.q: What do the Changing cards have in common?
good: Particles speed up or slow down.
The same stuff is in a different state.
Heat changes how the particles move.

flow.think: Can you think of something at home that goes through a change like this every day?

experiments.title: How Far Does One Drop Go? Cup after cup of colour
experiments.context: In this experiment you put one drop of food colour in water, and then keep passing a spoonful to a fresh cup. You find out how many cups the colour can colour, and what it means when the colour seems to be gone.
experiments.question: One drop of food colour turns a cup of water pink. If you keep mixing a spoonful of that pink water into a fresh cup of water, how many cups can the colour reach before you can no longer see it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many cups will still show some colour? Will a second colour, such as blue, go further or less far than red? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every cup has the same amount of water, ten teaspoons in all. Every spoonful passed on is exactly one level teaspoon, and you stir the same way each time. The cups sit on the same white paper in the same light. Only the colour changes between the red row and the blue row, so any difference comes from the colour.
results_table: Colour in this cup compared with cup 1
Can you see colour? (yes, faint or no)

materials.item: 7 clear cups or small tumblers (plastic is fine), each holding at least 100 millilitres so you can stir without spilling: six for the row, numbered 1 to 6 with a marker or tape, and one for plain water. For 2 to 4 children, give each child their own row of cups, one colour each
a teaspoon for measuring, and a second spoon for stirring
about 600 millilitres of water in a jug (each row of cups uses about 275 millilitres)
red food colour in a bottle with a dropper (if the bottle has no dropper, dip a toothpick in and let one drop fall off it), and a second colour such as blue or green
a sheet of plain white paper to stand the cups on
kitchen paper or a cloth to wipe up spills, and a tray or newspaper to work on

experiments.safety: Food colour stains clothes, skin and kitchen surfaces. Wear old clothes and wipe spills at once. Keep it away from the eyes. The coloured water is only for looking at. Do not drink it. Some children react to food dyes, so a child who does should only watch, and wear gloves or wash hands afterwards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for the red row. Then draw the row of cups and colour each cup as dark as you saw it. Do the same for the blue row.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for red colour (yours will be different)
cols: Colour in this cup compared with cup 1

setup.art: Six clear cups in a row on white paper, numbered 1 to 6, with ten teaspoons of water in cup 1 and nine teaspoons in each of cups 2 to 6.
setup.caption: 1. Number six cups. Put 10 teaspoons of water in cup 1 and 9 teaspoons in each other cup.

setup.art: A red food colour dropper held above cup 1 with a single drop falling into the water, and a spoon beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of colour in cup 1. Stir.

setup.art: A teaspoon of pink water being poured from cup 1 into cup 2, with an arrow from cup 1 to cup 2.
setup.caption: 3. Take one level teaspoon from cup 1 and stir it into cup 2.

setup.art: A hand carrying one teaspoon along the row from cup 2 to cup 3, then cup 3 to cup 4, with the colour getting paler in each cup.
setup.caption: 4. Keep going: one teaspoon from each cup into the next one.

setup.art: The finished row of cups going from deep pink to almost clear, with a plain water cup placed beside the last one for comparison.
setup.caption: 5. Look at the row from above. Put a plain water cup beside the last cup to compare.

flow.do: Show the cups, the colour and the spoon. Ask for a guess about how many cups will show colour, and for a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will put one drop of colour in a cup of water. Then we will pass one spoonful to the next cup, again and again. How many cups will have colour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One drop. Six cups. How many will show colour? Why do you think so?

ask.q: How many cups do you think will show colour, and why?
good: Only two, because the drop is so small.
All six, because colour never goes away.
Three or four, because the colour gets thinner each time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess two or three. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the colour test. You guess before you try.

flow.do: 1. Number the cups 1 to 6. 2. Stand them on the white paper in a row. 3. Put 10 teaspoons of water in cup 1. 4. Put 9 teaspoons in each of the other cups.
flow.say: Cup 1 gets ten spoons of water. Every other cup gets nine. We will count the spoons carefully, because we want each cup to hold the same amount.
flow.kid: Number the cups. Cup 1 gets 10 spoons of water. The rest get 9.
flow.parent: Measure with level teaspoons, not heaped ones. The nine spoons plus the one spoonful that comes in make ten, so every cup holds the same amount in the end.

flow.do: 1. Hold the dropper above cup 1. 2. Let one drop fall in. 3. Stir with the second spoon for 10 seconds. 4. Look at the colour from above.
flow.say: Hold the dropper over cup 1 and let one drop fall. Stir for ten seconds. What do you see? How much of the cup has the colour reached?
flow.kid: Let one drop fall into cup 1. Stir. What do you see?

ask.q: What do you see after you stir? What do you wonder?
good: The whole cup is pink.
One drop made all this colour.
Where did the colour go?

flow.parent: Cup 1 should be a strong pink or red. If it looks pale, add one more drop and write 2 drops in the table.

flow.do: 1. Use the teaspoon to take one level teaspoon from cup 1. 2. Stir it into cup 2 for 10 seconds. 3. Rinse the spoon. 4. Take one level teaspoon from cup 2 and stir it into cup 3. 5. Keep going to cup 6.
flow.say: Take one level spoonful from cup 1 into cup 2. Stir. Rinse the spoon. Now one spoonful from cup 2 into cup 3. Keep going, all the way to cup 6.
flow.kid: Move one spoonful from each cup to the next. Stir. Rinse the spoon.
flow.wait: Take your time and rinse the spoon each time, or the colours will mix.
flow.parent: The colour in each cup is one tenth of the colour in the cup before. Cup 3 holds one hundredth of cup 1, cup 4 one thousandth, and so on. A rinsed spoon keeps the test fair.

flow.do: 1. Look at the row from above, against the white paper. 2. For each cup, write yes, faint or no in the table. 3. Put a cup of plain water next to cup 6 and compare. 4. Look from the side too.
flow.say: Look at the row from above, then from the side. Which cups still have colour? Put plain water next to the last cup. Can you tell them apart?
flow.kid: Look at every cup. Write yes, faint or no. Compare the last cup with plain water.
flow.parent: Typically the colour fades out somewhere between cup 3 and cup 5 on white paper, depending on how strong your food colour is, so there is no right number. If the colour has gone by cup 2 or 3, begin again with 3 drops in cup 1 and note it in the table. If cup 6 is still quite bright, add cups 7 and 8. With 2 to 4 children, each runs one row (one colour each) and then you compare the rows; it is a good way to find which colour goes furthest. One child can be the spoon-carrier and one the stirrer, and swap roles for the second row. Hold the cups up to a window or white paper to judge.

check.q: Cup 6 looks clear. Is there still colour in it?
options: Yes, a tiny amount, spread so thinly you cannot see it
Yes, but it has all sunk to the bottom
check.why: Each spoonful carried a tenth of the colour forward, so cup 6 holds a hundred thousandth of the first cup's colour. The colour particles are still there (if nothing shows, it is because the eye cannot see so few), but too few in each spoonful to see. Picking 'gone' means trusting your eyes over the numbers. Picking 'sunk to the bottom' forgets that you stirred.

flow.do: 1. Pour out the red cups and rinse them. 2. Do the same test with the second colour, from cup 1 to cup 6. 3. Write what you see in a second row of the table.
flow.say: Now do exactly the same with the blue colour. Does it go further than the red, or less far? Write down what you see.
flow.kid: Repeat with the second colour. Does it go further or less far?
flow.parent: Different colours are made from different dyes, and some are stronger. So one colour often stays visible for one more cup than the other.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: one drop holds so many colour particles that they spread into many cups. What I saw: the pink faded cup by cup, and the last cup looked clear, perhaps a tiny bit different from plain water. Why: each spoonful carries a tenth of the colour, so there is less and less, but never exactly none.
flow.think: If the colour in cup 6 is still there, how could you prove it without looking?

experiments.title: The Squeeze Test: can air, water and a water-and-bubble mix be squashed?
experiments.context: In this experiment you use a syringe with no needle to squeeze air and water. You find out which one can be squashed, and what that tells you about the space between particles.
experiments.question: A syringe is full of air, and another is full of water. You seal the end and push the plunger as hard as you can. Which one squashes, and by how much?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How far will the plunger go in when it is full of air, and when it is full of water? What will happen if the water has a small bubble of air in it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same syringe, the same starting amount of 10 millilitres, the same finger seal and the same push each time. You try each test three times and use the middle number. Only what is inside the syringe changes.

materials.item: a plastic syringe with no needle, holding 10 or 20 millilitres, with a smooth plunger (a chemist sells these for a few rupees; a medicine-dosing syringe from a baby syrup also works)
a small bowl of water, and a cup of water for filling the syringe
a clean finger, or a small blob of modelling clay or a rubber eraser to press the tip into, to seal the end of the syringe
a few drops of cooking oil on a cloth, in case the plunger leaks
a notebook and a pencil for the results table
a towel to catch drips

experiments.safety: Use only a syringe with no needle. Never point a syringe at a face or an eye. Keep the small parts away from children under five. Hold the plunger firmly, because it can spring back. Work over a tray or in the kitchen sink, because the seal may leak and squirt water. Do not use a syringe that has been used for medicine unless it is washed well.
experiments.record: Fill in the table with the numbers. Then draw a picture of the air in the syringe before and after you push, showing the particles as dots.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results (yours will be different)
rows: Water with a small air bubble

setup.art: A syringe with the plunger pulled back to the 10 millilitre mark, full of air, with the tip sealed by a fingertip.
setup.caption: 1. Pull the plunger back to 10 millilitres. Seal the tip with a finger.

setup.art: A thumb pushing the plunger as far as it will go, with the 5 millilitre mark showing next to the end of the plunger.
setup.caption: 2. Push the plunger in as far as it will go. Read the mark.

setup.art: The syringe filled to 10 millilitres with water, tip pointing up and held under a cup of water, with a finger sealing the tip.
setup.caption: 3. Fill the syringe with water, with no bubbles. Seal the tip.

setup.art: A syringe with 9 millilitres of water and a small bubble of air at the top, sealed at the tip.
setup.caption: 4. Make a mix of water with a small bubble. Push again.

flow.do: Show your child the syringe. Pull the plunger out and in a few times. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This is a syringe with no needle. We will seal the end and push the plunger. What will happen with air inside? With water inside? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Seal the syringe. Push. What happens with air? With water? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen when you push the plunger, and why?
good: The air will squash, because it is light.
Neither will squash, because the end is blocked.
The water will squash more, because it is wet.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the squeeze test. You guess before you push.

flow.do: 1. Pull the plunger back to the 10 millilitre mark. 2. Press your fingertip tight over the end. 3. Push the plunger a little and let go. Does it spring back?
flow.say: Pull the plunger back to ten millilitres. Press your finger tight over the end. Push a little and let go. Does the plunger spring back? If it does, your seal is good.
flow.kid: Pull to 10. Seal the end with a finger. Push a little. Does it spring back?
flow.parent: If it does not spring back, air is leaking. Press the finger harder, or use a blob of clay over the tip. If the plunger sticks, rub a drop of cooking oil on the rubber.

flow.do: 1. Pull the plunger back to 10 millilitres again. 2. Seal the end. 3. Push the plunger in as far as you can and hold for 3 seconds. 4. Read the mark. 5. Do this three times.
flow.say: Seal the end and push the plunger in as far as you can. Hold for three seconds. Read the mark. Do it three times. Write each number down.
flow.kid: Seal. Push as hard as you can. Read the mark. Do it three times.

ask.q: What do you notice about the plunger when you let go?
good: It springs back.
It pushes my thumb out.
It feels like pushing on a spring.

flow.parent: Air usually squashes to between 3 and 6 millilitres, depending on how hard you push and how well your finger seals; a weak seal gives a smaller squash, so compare your three tries and use the middle number. The plunger springs back when you let go. With 2 to 4 children there is one syringe, so give roles: one pushes, one seals the tip, one reads the mark, one writes. Swap roles after each of the three tries so everyone pushes once, and note that a stronger child will squash it more, which is why the same person should push for all three tests in the table.

flow.do: 1. Fill a cup with water. 2. Dip the syringe tip in and pull the plunger back to 10 millilitres to draw in water. 3. Hold the tip up, tap out the bubbles, and push the plunger up until there is no air. 4. Seal the end. 5. Push as hard as you can.
flow.say: Draw up ten millilitres of water. Tap out the bubbles. Seal the end with your finger, and push as hard as you can. What do you see? Do it three times.
flow.kid: Fill with water. Tap out the bubbles. Seal. Push as hard as you can.
flow.parent: The plunger may move a tiny amount or not at all, and a finger seal may leak a drop. Write 0 or about 0. If water squirts out the sides, press the tip into a rubber eraser or clay instead of a finger. Tap out every bubble first, or you will be measuring the bubble.

check.q: The plunger hardly moved when the syringe was full of water. Why?
options: The water particles are touching, so there is no empty space to squash them into
The water is too heavy to move
The water particles are very big
check.why: In water, the particles are close together and touching. Pushing them closer takes a huge force, because there is no empty space for them to move into. Picking 'too heavy' mixes up weight and being squashable. Picking 'very big' is not the reason, because water particles are tiny.

flow.do: 1. Draw up 9 millilitres of water. 2. Pull the plunger back to 10 millilitres, to let in a small bubble of air. 3. Seal the end. 4. Push as hard as you can and read the mark. 5. Do it three times.
flow.say: Now put a small bubble of air in with the water. Seal the end and push. How far does the plunger go this time? What squashed, the water or the bubble?
flow.kid: Water plus a small bubble. Seal. Push. What squashed?
flow.parent: The mix should squash by less than the size of the bubble, because only the bubble can squash. This shows that the water was not squashing. The bubble was.

flow.do: 1. Look at your three results. 2. Fill in the 'How much it squashed' column. 3. Talk about which squashed and which did not.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. Which squashed the most? Which squashed the least? What do the particles in each one have to do?
flow.kid: Look at the table. Which squashed most? Which squashed least?
flow.parent: Air squashes a lot, water almost not at all, and water with a bubble squashes by about the bubble's size.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then ask them to draw the air particles before and after pushing.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think? What did you see? Why did it happen? Then draw the air particles before and after.
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why. Then draw the air particles.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: What I think: air has empty space between its particles. What I saw: the air squashed to about half and sprang back, and the water did not move. Why: air particles are far apart, so they can be pushed closer. Water particles already touch. In the drawing, the particles should be the same size before and after, just closer together after.
flow.think: If you kept squeezing the air in the syringe harder and harder, what do you think would stop you at last?

activities.title: Rice Tray Crowds: a model of a solid, a liquid and a gas
activities.context: In this activity you use a tray of rice as a model of particles. By shaking it three different ways, you make a crowd that behaves like a solid, a liquid and a gas.

materials.item: a steel plate or tray with a rim, such as a thali
2 cups of dry rice, or any small grains
a tiffin box or a container with a lid that closes tightly
a sheet of paper and a pencil for drawing

schedule.what: Shake the rice three ways and watch what it does. Then ask where the model gets things wrong.

activities.record: Draw three pictures of the rice: packed in rows, sliding in a pile, and flying about in the box. Write solid, liquid or gas under each.

setup.art: A steel plate with rice grains pressed together in a single neat layer and a hand shaking the plate a tiny bit.
setup.caption: 1. Spread rice in a neat packed layer on the plate. Shake the plate very gently.

setup.art: The same plate tilted with a heap of rice sliding down and spreading out.
setup.caption: 2. Tip the rice into a heap. Shake harder and tilt the plate.

setup.art: A closed tiffin box with a handful of rice grains inside, and a child shaking it hard with both hands.
setup.caption: 3. Put a handful of rice in a closed box. Shake it hard.

flow.do: 1. Spread rice grains in a single layer on the plate so they touch. 2. Shake the plate very gently from side to side. 3. Watch the grains.
flow.say: Pack the rice close, in a single layer. Shake the plate very gently. What do the grains do? Do they move around the plate?
flow.kid: Pack the rice close. Shake the plate gently. Watch the grains.

ask.q: What do the grains do when you shake gently?
good: They wobble on the spot.
They stay in the same places.
They jiggle but do not swap places.

flow.parent: The grains wobble a little but stay in their places. This is a model of a solid. Before shaking, ask your child to predict which of the three will make the most noise. With 2 to 4 children, each child shakes their own plate or box, or one shakes while another draws. Keep the rice on a tray, because grains on a smooth floor are slippery. Do not eat the rice afterwards.
flow.context: This is the first step of the rice tray model. You make a crowd that acts like a solid.

flow.do: 1. Tip the rice into a loose heap. 2. Shake the plate harder and tilt it a little. 3. Watch how the grains move.
flow.say: Tip the rice into a heap. Shake harder and tilt the plate. What do the grains do now? Do they stay in place?
flow.kid: Shake harder and tilt the plate. What do the grains do now?

ask.q: How is this crowd different from the first one?
good: The grains slide past each other.
The grains flow downhill.
The grains take the shape of the plate.

flow.parent: The grains slide over each other and flow to the low side. They stay close and keep touching. This is a model of a liquid.

flow.do: 1. Put a handful of rice in the tiffin box. 2. Close the lid tight. 3. Shake the box hard. 4. Listen, and feel the grains hit the walls.
flow.say: Put a handful of rice in the box and close it. Shake it hard. What can you hear and feel? Where are the grains now?
flow.kid: Put some rice in the box. Close it. Shake hard. Listen.

ask.q: What do you hear and feel when the grains hit the box?
good: Rattling on every wall.
A push on my hands.
The grains fly all over the box.

flow.parent: The grains hit all the walls and the lid, and you hear and feel it. Shake harder, and it is louder. This is a model of gas pressure.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Then ask your child to draw the three crowds and write solid, liquid or gas under each.
flow.say: Rice grains are not particles. They are big, they touch, and they are solid. Where does this model get things wrong for a gas?
flow.kid: Where does the rice model get things wrong?

check.q: Where does the rice model get a gas wrong?
options: The grains in a gas model should be much further apart, with nothing between them
check.why: Real gas particles are very far apart for their size, with empty space between them. In the box, the grains are close, and there is air in between. Picking 'too round' is about shape, which is not the main problem. Picking 'not a gas' misses the point of a model: it does not have to be a gas to show how gas acts.

flow.think: What would you need to change to make the box a better model of a gas?

activities.title: Full Jar, Not Really Full: chana, mustard and water
activities.context: In this activity you fill a jar with big grains, and then find out that it still has room for small seeds and water. It is a model of the empty space between particles.

materials.item: a clear measuring jug with millilitre marks, holding at least 500 millilitres (or a clear tumbler with a pen mark, and a steel spoon of known size, where 1 teaspoon is about 5 millilitres)
about 400 millilitres of chana dal or whole chana
about 200 millilitres of mustard seeds or ragi
a cup of water and a measuring cup or a spoon for measuring
a tray to catch spills, and a pencil and paper

activities.safety: Use food that you will not eat afterwards, because it gets mixed and wet. Small seeds and beans can choke a child under five, so keep them out of reach.

schedule.what: Fill the jar with big grains, then small seeds, then water. Measure how much each one added.

activities.record: A table with three rows: big grains, small seeds added, water added. Write the amount of each in millilitres and the total.

setup.art: A clear jug filled to the 300 millilitre line with chana dal, with a tray under it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the jug to the 300 millilitre line with chana.

setup.art: Mustard seeds being poured slowly into the jug of chana, with a hand tapping the side of the jug.
setup.caption: 2. Pour mustard seeds in slowly. Tap the jug until no more fit.

setup.art: A cup of water being poured slowly into the same jug until it reaches the top, with the water seen between the seeds.
setup.caption: 3. Pour water in slowly. Measure how much goes in.

flow.do: 1. Fill the jug to the 300 millilitre line with chana. 2. Shake it gently so it settles. 3. Top up to the line if needed. 4. Ask your child to guess how much more would fit.
flow.say: The jug is full of chana to the 300 line. Is it really full? How many millilitres of mustard seeds do you think we can still add? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The jug is full of chana. Can anything more fit? Why?

ask.q: Is the jug really full? What could still fit?
good: Small seeds could slide between the chana.
Nothing, because it is full.
Water could go in the gaps.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write down the guess in millilitres.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Full Jar activity. You fill the jug with big grains, and guess.

flow.do: 1. Measure out 200 millilitres of mustard seeds. 2. Pour them slowly onto the chana. 3. Tap the jug gently. 4. Stop when no more go in without lifting the level above the 300 millilitre line. 5. Measure the seeds that are left over.
flow.say: Pour the mustard seeds in slowly. Tap the jug so they slide into the gaps. Stop when no more will go in. How many millilitres went in?
flow.kid: Pour in the seeds slowly. Tap the jug. Stop when no more go in.
flow.parent: Typically 60 to 100 millilitres of seeds go in, though it depends on the grains (split chana dal packs closer than whole chana). If the numbers differ from yours, that is fine, and what matters is that some went in. With 2 to 4 children, one pours, one taps, one reads the jug and one writes; each guesses first. Work out the amount that went in by subtracting what is left over from 200.

flow.do: 1. Measure 100 millilitres of water. 2. Pour it slowly onto the grains and seeds. 3. Stop when the water reaches the top. 4. Measure the water left over.
flow.say: Is the jug really full now? Pour water in very slowly. How much goes in? Where do you think it goes?
flow.kid: Pour in water very slowly. How much goes in?
flow.parent: About 30 to 70 millilitres of water usually go in. Pour slowly, or bubbles will block the gaps.

check.q: Water still went into a jug that looked full of grains and seeds. Where did it go?
options: Into the tiny gaps between the grains and seeds
It soaked into the grains and made them vanish
check.why: Even after the small seeds filled the big gaps, there were still tiny gaps between the seeds, and water slid into them. Picking 'made them vanish' ignores that the grains are still there. Picking 'made the jug bigger' forgets that the jug is hard and cannot change size.

flow.do: Add up the three amounts. Compare the total with 300 millilitres. Then talk about what this shows.
flow.say: Add up the amounts. The jug only holds 500 millilitres. How much did you fit in? What do you think this tells us about empty space?
flow.kid: Add up the three amounts. How much did you fit in?

ask.q: What does this show about empty space between things?
good: Big things leave gaps for small things.
Even when it looks full, there is room.
Small things fit between big things.

flow.think: Particles of different sizes fit into each other's gaps in the same way. Where have you seen small things fit between big things?

activities.title: Substance or Mixture? Read the labels in your kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you look at things from your kitchen and read their labels. You find which are nearly one substance and which are clear mixtures.

materials.item: 10 things from the kitchen, such as a sugar packet, a salt packet, a bottle of mineral water, a tea packet, a milk packet, aluminium foil and a steel spoon
a sheet of paper with two columns, one for nearly one substance and one for mixture
a pencil

schedule.what: Pick ten things. Guess substance or mixture. Check the labels. Sort them.

activities.record: A two-column sheet. In the first column, write the things that seem to be one substance. In the second, write the mixtures. Next to each, write your reason.

setup.art: Ten kitchen things on a table: a sugar packet, a salt packet, a bottle of water, a tea packet, a milk packet, a steel spoon and aluminium foil.
setup.caption: 1. Line up ten things. Guess whether each is one substance or a mixture.

setup.art: A child reading the list of ingredients on the back of a salt packet.
setup.caption: 2. Read the label on each packet. Count the ingredients.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns, and the kitchen things sorted into them.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the things into two columns.

flow.do: Line up the ten things. Ask your child to guess for each one: is it one substance, or a mixture? Write the guess next to each name.
flow.say: Here are ten things. Which do you think are made of just one kind of stuff? Which are a mix of different kinds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the ten things. Guess one substance or a mixture. Why?

ask.q: Which one are you sure is a mixture, and why?
good: The tea, because I can see leaves and bits.
The milk, because it has fat and water.
The air, because it has several gases.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A label that lists more than one thing is a sign of a mixture. Do not taste anything to test it. With 2 to 4 children, each picks five things, guesses and reads the labels, and then swaps to check one another.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sorting activity. You guess before you check.

flow.do: 1. Read the label of each packet. 2. Count the ingredients in each. 3. For things without labels, such as the spoon, ask what it is made of. 4. Write the number of ingredients.
flow.say: Read the label on each packet. How many ingredients does it list? A label with many ingredients is a mixture. What does the sugar packet say?
flow.kid: Read the label on each packet. How many ingredients does it list?
flow.parent: Sugar lists one ingredient. Salt often lists salt, iodine and a small amount of something to keep it dry. A steel spoon is a mixture of iron with a little carbon and other metals. Foil is nearly all aluminium.

flow.do: 1. Sort the things into two columns. 2. Write the reason next to each one. 3. Mark anything that is nearly one substance but has a tiny extra bit.
flow.say: Sort the ten things into two columns. Put one reason next to each. Which ones were hard to decide?
flow.kid: Sort the things into two columns. Write one reason for each.
flow.parent: Some answers are in between. That is fine. Scientists use 'nearly pure' for something that is almost all one substance.

check.q: Salt lists salt and a tiny bit of iodine. Is it one substance or a mixture?
options: Nearly one substance, with a tiny extra bit
A mixture that is half salt and half iodine
check.why: Table salt is almost all one substance, with a tiny amount of other things added. Scientists would say it is a mixture, but a very pure one. Picking 'half and half' is wrong, because the iodine is only a tiny part. Everything has particles, so the third answer is wrong.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Why can't we say for sure that any packet is one pure substance?
flow.kid: Why is it hard to find a perfectly pure substance?
flow.think: Why might a scientist need special equipment to make a really pure substance?

activities.title: Draw the Particles: six things and one rule book
activities.context: In this activity you draw the particles of six things at home, using five rules. Then you swap with a partner, check each other's drawings, and find what a drawing leaves out.

materials.item: 6 sheets of paper, or one large sheet folded in six
a pencil, and coloured pencils or crayons
a partner, such as a parent, a brother or a sister

schedule.what: Draw six things as particles. Swap drawings and check them against the rules. Fix one drawing.

activities.record: Six particle drawings: a steel spoon, water in a glass, steam, air in a football, set ghee from the fridge and ghee melted in a hot pan. Each one has the name under it.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with six boxes, each with a circle drawn inside and the name of a thing under it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six boxes. Write one thing under each.

setup.art: A circle with particles drawn as dots in neat rows for a spoon, with a short arrow on each to show jiggle.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the particles in each box using the rules.

setup.art: Two children swapping their sheets and checking them with a ruler and a list of rules.
setup.caption: 3. Swap your sheet with a partner. Check each other's drawings.

flow.do: Read the five rules to your child. 1. All particles of one substance look the same. 2. Solid particles touch and sit in neat rows. 3. Liquid particles touch but are jumbled. 4. Gas particles are far apart. 5. Add small arrows to show how the particles move.
flow.say: Here are five rules for drawing particles. Say them back to me in your own words. Which rule would be hardest to draw?
flow.kid: Listen to the five rules. Say them in your own words.

ask.q: Which rule do you think is the hardest to draw?
good: Showing how fast they move.
Drawing them far apart in a gas.
Making all the particles look the same.

flow.parent: Write the rules where you can see them. Rules: same look, solid rows, liquid jumble, gas far apart, arrows for movement.
flow.context: This is the first step of the particle drawing activity. You learn five rules before you draw.

flow.do: Draw six boxes on paper. Draw the particles in each box. The six are a steel spoon, water, steam, football air, set ghee from the fridge and hot melted ghee.
flow.say: Draw the particles in each box. Use the rules. Think about how close they are and how they move. Add small arrows.
flow.kid: Draw the particles in each box. Use the rules. Add arrows.
flow.parent: Let your child draw first, and do not correct while they draw. For ghee, the picture changes from rows to jumble. Ask which rule they are using for each. In hot weather ghee on the shelf is already soft or runny, so use ghee that has been in the fridge. Each child can draw alone and then swap with one other, so it works with 2 to 4 children or just you and one parent.

check.q: In your drawing, how are the steam particles different from the water particles?
check.why: Steam and water are the same substance, with the same particles. In steam, the particles are very far apart and move fast. In water, they are close and slide. Picking 'bigger' is a common mistake: the particles do not grow. Picking 'different substance' forgets that steam is just hot water gas.

flow.do: 1. Swap your sheet with a partner. 2. Check each drawing against the five rules. 3. Put a tick when a rule is followed. 4. Put a question mark when it is not.
flow.say: Swap with your partner. Check each box against the rules. Tick if a rule is followed. Put a question mark if not. Tell your partner why.
flow.kid: Swap drawings. Check each box. Tick or question mark.

ask.q: Which rule was easiest to break by mistake?
good: Showing the particles all the same.
Drawing gas particles too close.
Forgetting the arrows.

flow.parent: Aim for kind feedback: one tick and one idea for each drawing.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose one drawing and fix it. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Pick one drawing and fix it. Then tell me, what does a drawing like this leave out?
flow.kid: Fix one drawing. What does a drawing leave out?
flow.think: A drawing is flat and still. What is real about particles that a flat, still picture cannot show well?

projects.title: A Picture Book of the Three Crowds: teach a younger child
projects.safety: A grown-up uses the stapler, or the pages can be tied with thread. Keep the stapler away from small children.
projects.context: In this project you make a small picture book that explains solids, liquids and gases to a younger child. You read it to them and find out what they ask.

materials.item: 5 sheets of plain paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread to make a small book
pencils and coloured pencils or crayons
your results and drawings from the other tests in this unit
a younger child, such as a brother, a sister, a cousin or a neighbour, to read to
a ruler and a pencil to write your questions

schedule.what: Plan eight pages. Draw the cover and the solid, liquid and gas pages.
Draw the changing page, the squashing page and the smell page. Write the words.
Read the book to a younger child. Write down their questions. Improve one page.

projects.record: The finished picture book, and a list of the questions the younger child asked.

setup.art: A small folded paper book with a cover that says The Three Crowds and a drawing of rice grains on a tray.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and tie your paper into a small book.

setup.art: An open book showing a page with particles in neat rows, a page with particles jumbled and a page with particles far apart.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one page each for a solid, a liquid and a gas.

setup.art: A child reading the book aloud to a smaller child, with the smaller child pointing at a drawing.
setup.caption: 3. Read the book to a younger child. Write down what they ask.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper into a book. 2. Plan the eight pages: cover, solid, liquid, gas, changing, squashing, smell, and what is in the gaps. 3. Draw the cover and the first three pages.
flow.say: Plan your book first. Eight pages. Which three crowds will you draw first? What example from home will you use for each?
flow.kid: Plan eight pages. Draw the cover and the solid, liquid and gas pages.
flow.parent: Encourage real examples from the tests: the rice tray, the syringe and the cups of colour. With 2 to 4 children, each draws two or three pages of the same book and they read it together. If there is no younger child nearby, read it to a parent or grandparent, and ask them to pretend to be five years old.
flow.context: This is the first step of the picture book project. You plan and start the pages.

flow.do: 1. Draw and write the changing page, the squashing page and the smell page. 2. Use the words particle, gap and pressure. 3. Write one sentence on each page.
flow.say: Now the other pages. Write one sentence on each. Use the words particle and gap. Explain it so a six year old could follow.
flow.kid: Draw and write the other pages. One sentence on each page.

ask.q: How will you explain a gap to a younger child?
good: Empty space between the particles.
Like the room between chairs in a hall.
A place where there is nothing.

flow.parent: Each sentence should be 12 words or fewer. If your child uses a hard word, ask them to explain it in a plain way.

flow.do: 1. Read the book to a younger child. 2. Ask them to point to the page they like best. 3. Write down every question they ask.
flow.say: Read the book to your younger friend. Stop at each page and ask what they think. Write down their questions.
flow.kid: Read your book to a younger child. Write down their questions.
flow.parent: Do not rush to answer. Young children often ask the best questions, such as 'what is between the particles?'

flow.do: 1. Pick the one question you could not answer well. 2. Look up the answer, or ask a grown-up. 3. Add a new page with the answer.
flow.say: Choose the question that was hardest. Find an answer. Add a new page to your book. Write the answer in plain words.
flow.kid: Pick the hardest question. Find the answer. Add a page.
flow.think: Why is explaining something to someone else a good way to find what you do not yet understand?

challenges.title: Prove That Air Is Something
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Many people think air is nothing. You must find a way to show that the air in your house is real stuff, using things from your kitchen.
challenges.problem: A friend says the room is empty because there is nothing in the air. She will not believe you if you only say that air is made of particles. Find a way to show her that air is something real, without using a syringe.
constraints: You may use only things from your kitchen and your home.
You must show the result in a way your friend can see, feel or hear.
You may not use a syringe or a pump.
Your test must work again if your friend asks you to repeat it.
challenges.safety: Hit the end of the ruler with a flat hand, not hard, and keep your face away from it. A wooden ruler can snap, so use a plastic one or a thin flat stick. Keep plastic bags and balloons away from the faces of small children, and put burst balloon pieces in the bin, because they are a choking risk. Wipe up spilt water at once.
materials: a bowl or a bucket of water
a clear plastic glass or tumbler (plastic will not break)
a balloon (a packet is a few rupees at a stationery shop)
a ruler, a large flat sheet of newspaper, and a few tissues or a crumpled piece of paper
general: Push an upside-down glass straight down into a bucket of water. The air inside stops the water from coming in, and you see the water level stay low inside the glass.
Blow up a balloon and tie it. Squeeze it, and feel the springy air push back. Let the air out slowly on your hand and feel it.
Fill a plastic carry bag with air by scooping it, twist the top closed, and squeeze. It resists, like a cushion.
creative: Put a ruler on a table with about a third of it hanging over the edge. Cover the rest with a sheet of newspaper and smooth it flat. Hit the hanging end of the ruler and watch the air press the paper down.

Push a crumpled tissue to the bottom of a dry glass, turn it upside down and push it straight down into the water. Lift it out and feel the tissue. It stays dry, because the air in the glass held the water out. With 2 to 4 children, each tries it with a different thing at the bottom and compares.
Tilt the upside-down glass slowly under the water, and watch the air escape as bubbles that you can count.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own test. Draw it, try it, and show your friend. Which of your tests would be the most convincing for a person who does not believe in air? Why?

setup.art: An upside-down glass pushed straight down into a bucket of water, with the water level staying low inside the glass.
setup.caption: 1. Push a glass upside down into water. See what the air does.

setup.art: A child squeezing a balloon and feeling the air push back against both hands.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze a closed balloon. Feel the air push back.

setup.art: A ruler under a sheet of newspaper on a table, with a hand hitting the end of the ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Try the ruler and newspaper trick.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Look at the things. Ask your child to think of two ways to show that air is something.
flow.say: Your friend says the room is empty. How could you show her that air is real stuff? Think of two ways before you try anything.
flow.kid: Your friend says air is nothing. Think of two ways to show her.

ask.q: What can air do that nothing could do?
good: It can push on things.
It can stop water coming in.
It can make a balloon round.

flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge Prove That Air Is Something. You plan.

flow.do: 1. Try the first idea. 2. Write down what you see, hear or feel. 3. Try a second idea. 4. Change one thing and try again.
flow.say: Try your first idea. What do you see, hear or feel? Then try your second. Change one thing and try again. Write down what happens.
flow.kid: Try your first idea. Write what you see. Then try another.
flow.parent: Water in the tumbler test: push the glass straight down, not tilted. The water level inside should stay low.

flow.do: 1. Choose the test that was most convincing. 2. Show it to a family member or friend who has not seen it. 3. Ask them what they think it shows.
flow.say: Pick your best test. Show someone who has not seen it. Ask them what they think it shows. Did they believe you?
flow.kid: Pick your best test. Show someone. Did they believe you?

check.q: A glass pushed upside down into water keeps the water out. What does this show?
options: Air takes up space and cannot be in the same place as water
check.why: The air in the glass has to be somewhere, so it stays inside and keeps the water out. This shows air is a real thing that takes up space. Picking 'glass is lighter' is about floating, not about air. The third answer is a silly one, but it is a reminder to give a reason from the test.

flow.think: What is the best evidence for something you cannot see?

flow.do: Ask your child to write down one sentence on how they know air is real.
flow.say: Write one sentence that proves air is real. Use something you saw or felt today.
flow.kid: Write one sentence that shows air is real.
flow.parent: A good sentence names the test and what it showed, such as 'The glass kept the water out, so air takes up space.'

videos.title: Part(icles) of Your World: Crash Course Kids #3.2
videos.why: A short, lively explanation for children that everything is made of particles too small to see.
videos.check: A parent should preview it first.

videos.title: States of Matter and Particle Theory for Kids
videos.why: To see particles drawn as moving dots in a solid, a liquid and a gas, and to see them speed up when heated.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

videos.why: To see how sealed steam builds up pressure, and how the weight and safety valve let it out.

quiz.p: What is the main difference between a solid, a liquid and a gas of the same substance?
opts: How the particles are arranged and how they move
quiz.why: The particles are the same. In a solid they are held in place. In a liquid they slide. In a gas they fly about, far apart.

quiz.p: Meera pours water from a bottle into a wide bowl. Why does the water take the shape of the bowl, but still make the same amount?
opts: The particles slide past each other but stay close
The particles are fixed in rows
quiz.why: Liquid particles slide, so the liquid can change shape. They stay touching, so the amount stays the same.

quiz.p: Why can air be squeezed into a smaller space?
opts: Its particles are far apart, with empty space between them
quiz.why: The particles are not squashed. They are pushed closer together, into the empty space.

quiz.p: A drop of colour is stirred into a cup, and a spoonful of that is stirred into another cup, again and again. The last cup looks clear. What is the best description?
opts: The colour is there, spread so thin you cannot see it
The colour is at the bottom of the first cup
quiz.why: Each spoonful carries a tenth of the colour onward. Some always goes on, even when too faint to see.
A gas pushes on its container because its particles hit the walls and bounce back.

quiz.p: Sambar is best described as which of these?
quiz.why: Sambar is made of several substances, such as water, dal and spices, mixed together.

quiz.p: Which change makes the particles of a solid move faster?
quiz.why: Heat is movement of particles. A warmer solid has particles that jiggle harder.

quiz.p: The particles in a gas hardly pull on each other at all.
quiz.why: True. Gas particles are so far apart that they barely pull on each other, so they fly free.

quiz.p: A model of particles uses tiny balls. What is true about this model?
opts: It is useful, but not exactly right
quiz.why: The balls help us think, but real atoms are fuzzy. All models have limits.

quiz.p: Which of these makes a smell spread faster across a room?
quiz.why: Moving air carries the smell particles much faster than they could spread by themselves.

quiz.p: A gas can be made of exactly the same particles as a liquid.
quiz.why: True. Steam and liquid water are both made of water particles.

quiz.p: Why was the idea of flying gas particles so useful to scientists?
opts: It explained why heating a gas raises its pressure
quiz.why: Faster particles hit harder, so a hotter gas pushes more. The older idea of fixed particles could not explain this.

items.p: Which sentence describes the particles in a solid best?
opts: They are far apart and fly about
They touch their neighbours and are held in place, jiggling on the spot
items.why: In a solid the particles are close and held in place by pulls between them. Picking the first describes a gas. Picking the last describes a liquid.

items.p: Neha seals the end of a syringe full of air and pushes the plunger. It goes in about half way. What does this tell you about air?
opts: There is empty space between the air particles
items.why: The particles moved closer together into the empty space between them. Air is made of particles, so it is not nothing. The particles do not get squashed, they just get closer.

items.p: Why does the steam from a kettle spread out until you cannot see it?
opts: Gas particles fly about and spread into all the space they can reach
Steam is lighter than the kitchen
items.why: Gas particles are free to fly in every direction, so a gas spreads out to fill the space it is in. Particles do not melt away.

items.p: Ice, water and steam are three states of one substance. What is the same in all three?
items.why: All three are made of the same water particles. What changes is the distance between them and how fast they move.

items.p: Why does a football feel hard when it is pumped up?
opts: Nothing is hitting the inside wall
Air particles hit the inside wall very often and push outwards
The air has turned into a solid
items.why: A huge number of air particles hit the inside wall every second. Together they push outwards, and that makes the ball hard. The air is still a gas.

items.p: The particles in a steel spoon are completely still.
items.why: False. The particles in a solid jiggle on the spot all the time. They just do not swap places.

items.p: The water particles in ice are a different kind from the water particles in steam.
items.why: False. They are exactly the same particles. Only how close they are and how fast they move is different.

items.p: A very tiny piece that a substance is made of, far too small to see, is a ____.
items.why: Everything is made of particles, and they are far too small to see with the eyes alone.

items.p: The push of a gas on the walls of its container is called gas ____.
items.why: Gas pressure comes from countless particles hitting the walls and bouncing off.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: what an object is made of
one kind of stuff, made of one kind of particle
two or more substances mixed together
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words are used all through the unit. A material can be a substance or a mixture.

items.p: Sort these things by what state they are in at room temperature.
items: coconut oil on a warm day
items.a: see items
items.why: A solid keeps its shape, a liquid takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill it.

items.p: Put the steps of the colour dilution test in order.
items: Stir one spoonful into the next cup of water
Put one drop of colour in cup 1 and stir
Number the cups and measure water into them
Look along the row and compare with plain water
a: Number the cups and measure water into them
Put one drop of colour in cup 1 and stir
Stir one spoonful into the next cup of water
Look along the row and compare with plain water
items.why: First set up the cups, then add the drop, then pass the colour on, and last compare the cups.

items.p: One drop of food colour can turn a whole cup of water pink. Why can one small drop do this?
items.a: A drop holds a huge number of colour particles. They spread out through the water, so there are some in every part of the cup.
items.why: A strong answer says the drop is made of a huge number of tiny particles that spread through all the water.

items.p: Explain to a younger child why you can squash air in a syringe but not water.
items.a: Air particles are far apart, with lots of empty space between them, so you can push them closer. Water particles already touch, so there is nowhere for them to go.
items.why: A strong answer names the empty space between air particles and says the water particles are already touching.

items.p: Draw the particles in steam. Show how far apart they are and add arrows to show how they move.
items.a: Small circles far apart, each with a long arrow in a different direction.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the particles far apart with arrows in all directions, because steam is a gas.
items.art: A large empty circle, like the view through a magnifying glass.

items.p: A pressure cooker is heated, and the steam cannot escape. What happens to the push of the steam on the lid?
opts: It gets bigger, because the particles fly faster and hit the lid harder
items.why: Heat makes the steam particles move faster. They hit the lid harder and more often, so the pressure goes up. This is also why the lid will not open until the cooker cools.

items.p: A jar is full to the top with big chana, and then small mustard seeds slide in between them. What does this show?
opts: The chana had gaps between the grains
items.why: Small things fit into the gaps between big things. In the same way, small particles can fit into the gaps between bigger ones.

items.p: A smell takes minutes to cross a room, though air particles fly at hundreds of metres a second. What is the best reason?
opts: The smell particles keep colliding with air particles and zigzag
The smell particles are very slow
Smells are not made of particles
items.why: A smell particle hits an air particle billions of times each second, and changes direction each time. So it travels only a little way from where it started. Moving air from a fan carries it much faster.

items.p: A balloon left in a hot car bursts. What is the best reason?
opts: The hot air particles fly faster and hit the skin harder
The rubber melts into the air
items.why: Heat makes the particles faster, so they hit the balloon harder and more often. The pressure goes up until the skin gives way. The particles do not grow.

items.p: A gas is squashed into half the space. What changes?
opts: Each particle is half the size
The particles are closer together and hit the walls more often
items.why: The same particles are now in half the space. They are closer, so they reach the walls twice as often. The particles themselves do not change.

items.p: Which of these is a mixture?
items.why: Sambar has water, dal, vegetables, tamarind and spices. The other two are very nearly one substance.

items.p: Which statement about an atom is correct?
opts: An atom is a solid ball with no empty space
An atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny nucleus in the middle
All atoms are the same size and kind
items.why: An atom is mostly empty space. The nucleus is about a hundred thousand times smaller than the whole atom. There are about a hundred different kinds of atom.

items.p: A heap of dry rice that pours like a liquid is a liquid.
items.why: False. Each grain of rice is a solid. A heap of grains can flow, but the grains keep their shape.

items.p: If you heat a gas in a closed container, the pressure goes up.
items.why: True. Faster particles hit the walls harder and more often.

items.p: The slow spreading of particles through a gas or a liquid, with no stirring, is called ____.
items.why: Diffusion happens because particles move and collide, and spread out over time.

items.p: Is each description true of the particles in a solid or of the particles in a gas?
items: fly in straight lines until they hit something
items.a: see items
items.why: In a solid the particles are close and held in place. In a gas they are far apart and free.

items.p: Match each thing you can see to the idea it shows.
pairs: Particles jiggle harder and break free
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each everyday event is one of the ideas of the particle model.

items.p: Put the steps of the squeeze test in order.
items: Seal the end with a finger
Pull the plunger back to 10 millilitres
Push the plunger in as far as you can and read the mark
Write the numbers in the table
a: Pull the plunger back to 10 millilitres
Seal the end with a finger
Push the plunger in as far as you can and read the mark
Write the numbers in the table
items.why: The syringe must have its starting amount first. Then you seal it, push it and record.

items.p: A cup of water looks clear, but it came from the sixth cup of a dilution test. Why can the colour still be there?
items.a: Each cup carried only a tenth of the colour forward, so the sixth cup has very little. The colour particles are spread so thinly that we cannot see them, but they are not gone.
items.why: A strong answer says the colour is spread very thin, but a tiny share of a huge number of particles is still some particles.

items.p: A friend says air is nothing, because you cannot see it. Give one reason why she is wrong.
items.a: A balloon filled with air feels springy when you squeeze it. An upside-down glass pushed into water keeps the water out. So air takes up space and pushes.
items.why: A strong answer names a test, and says what it shows about air being real stuff.

items.p: Explain why heating a gas in a sealed container makes the pressure go up.
items.a: Heat makes the gas particles move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the push on the walls is bigger.
items.why: A strong answer says the particles are faster and hit the walls harder and more often.

items.p: Draw a closed box of gas. Show the particles and arrows that show what makes pressure on one wall.
items.a: A box with particles far apart. Arrows show some particles hitting the wall.
items.why: A strong drawing shows particles hitting the wall, because the hits make the pressure.
items.art: A large empty square with thick walls.

items.p: Meena and Farhan are talking about the particles in a steel spoon.

views.says: A steel spoon does not move, so its particles are completely still.
The particles in a spoon jiggle on the spot. If you heat the spoon, they jiggle harder.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing that the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Farhan, because a hot spoon is evidence the particles move, since heat is movement. It also says Meena is right that the spoon as a whole does not move, and that the particles stay in their places.
items.why: Both have part of it. The spoon stays where it is, and its particles stay in their places, as Meena says. But they jiggle on the spot all the time, as Farhan says, and heating makes the jiggle bigger.

items.p: 100 millilitres of mustard seeds are poured into 100 millilitres of big dal. What total is most likely?
opts: About 170 millilitres, because the seeds fill gaps
items.why: Small seeds slip into the gaps between the big grains, so the total is less than the two added together.

items.p: A syringe holds 10 millilitres of air. It is squashed to 2 millilitres. About how many times as many air particles are there in each millilitre now?
items.why: The same particles are in one fifth of the space. 10 divided by 2 is 5, so there are 5 times as many in each millilitre.

items.p: The air in a bicycle tyre is at about three times the push of the outside air, at the same warmth. What does this mean for the particles?
opts: There are about three times as many particles in the same space
The particles are three times bigger
The particles are three times slower
items.why: At the same warmth, the particles move at the same speed. The extra push comes from more particles hitting the wall each second.

items.p: A scientist draws particles as tiny round balls. What is the most honest way to describe this drawing?
opts: A useful model that is not exactly true
A wrong idea that nobody uses
items.why: The balls explain a lot, but real atoms are fuzzy and have no sharp edge. Scientists keep using the model while knowing its limits.

items.p: A sealed pressure cooker has steam at twice the push of the outside air. Why is it hard to open?
opts: The push of the steam on the lid is much bigger than the push of the air outside
The steam makes the lid heavier
items.why: The steam pushes outwards on the lid harder than the outside air pushes inwards. The lid will not open until the push inside falls, which happens as the cooker cools.

items.p: Heating a solid makes its particles grow bigger.
items.why: False. The particles stay the same size. They jiggle harder and push each other a little further apart, so the whole solid takes up a little more room.

items.p: Gas pressure is made by particles ____ the walls of the container.
items.why: Each hit is tiny, but a countless number of hits make a steady push.

items.p: Does the rice tray model show each idea well, or is it misleading?
items: Grains in a packed tray wobble in place like a solid
Grains in a closed box hit the walls like gas particles
Rice grains are huge compared with real particles
Grains in a shaken box are close together, but gas particles are far apart
Grains slide over each other like particles in a liquid
items.a: see items
items.why: A model shows some things well and others badly. Knowing both is part of using it well.

items.p: Put these in order of how fast their particles move, from slowest to fastest.
items.why: The hotter a substance, the faster its particles move on average.

items.p: You halve the space a sealed gas is in, at the same warmth. What happens to the number of hits on the walls each second? Why?
items.a: There are more hits. The same particles are in half the space, so each one reaches a wall about twice as often.
items.why: A strong answer says the particles reach the walls more often because there is less room.

items.p: A friend draws the air in a football as particles touching each other in neat rows. Give two things that are wrong with the drawing.
items.a: Gas particles are far apart, not touching. They fly about in all directions, so they are not in neat rows.
items.why: A strong answer says gas particles are far apart and move freely, not in rows.

items.p: Salt dissolves in a full glass of water, and the water level hardly changes. Explain why.
items.a: The salt particles fit into the empty gaps between the water particles, so they take up very little extra room.
items.why: A strong answer says the salt particles fit between the water particles.

items.p: Why might a good scientific idea be ignored for a very long time?
items.a: People may already have an idea that seems to work. A new idea may need careful measuring and maths, and it may come from someone people do not listen to.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason such as an old idea that seems to work, or a new idea without enough evidence yet.

items.p: Draw two boxes of gas of the same size. Put half as many particles in the second box. Label which has the lower pressure.
items.a: The first box has twice as many particles, the second has half. The second is labelled lower pressure.
items.why: A strong drawing has fewer particles in the second box and labels it lower pressure.
items.art: Two large empty squares side by side.

items.p: Draw one drop of colour in a cup of water just after it falls in and a minute after it is stirred. Show the colour particles.
items.a: First picture: the colour particles are clumped together in one place. Second picture: they are spread out through the whole cup.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the colour particles clumped, and then spread out.
items.art: Two large empty circles side by side, each a top-down view of a cup.

items.p: Asha and Ravi are talking about a table.

views.says: A table is solid, so there is no empty space inside it.
Even a table is mostly empty space, because atoms are mostly empty space. It feels hard because the atoms push on each other.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from the unit. Then say one thing that the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Ravi, because atoms are mostly empty space, and the hardness comes from the push between atoms. It also says Asha is right that a table is a solid, with its particles held in place.
items.why: Both are partly right. A table is a solid, as Asha says. But it is full of gaps, as Ravi says, because even atoms are mostly empty space.

applications: Pressure cookers use sealed steam at about twice the push of outside air, so water boils at about 120 degrees Celsius and food cooks faster.
Bicycle and car tyres hold air at several times the push of the outside air, which keeps them firm.
LPG cylinders hold gas squeezed so hard that most of it turns into a liquid inside the cylinder.
Medicine inhalers and spray bottles push a gas to carry a fine mist of medicine into the lungs.
Perfume, incense and air fresheners work because their particles spread through the air by diffusion and air currents.
Weather balloons are filled with a gas that is lighter than air, and they swell as they rise, because the air outside gets thinner.
Scuba divers carry air squeezed into a steel tank, so that they can breathe for an hour underwater.
Engineers use computer models of particles to design new materials, such as stronger steel and better batteries.
Chemists make pure substances, such as medicines, by separating one kind of particle from a mixture.
Hospitals use oxygen gas squeezed into cylinders to help people breathe.
A refrigerator moves heat by squeezing and letting go of a gas inside its pipes.

open_questions.q: Is there a smallest thing, with nothing smaller inside it?
open_questions.why_open: Atoms are made of smaller parts, and those parts are described as ripples in fields. Physicists do not know if there is a last, smallest level.

open_questions.q: Is the empty space between particles really empty?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists describe even empty space as having fields in it. They still argue about what, if anything, that means for how we should picture it.

open_questions.q: Why do atoms of only about a hundred kinds make everything we know?
open_questions.why_open: We know how atoms are built and how they join. Why the universe has just these kinds is part of a bigger question that nobody has answered.

open_questions.q: What is the best picture of a particle: a ball, a cloud, or a ripple?
open_questions.why_open: Each picture works for some questions and fails for others. Physicists still use all three, and they do not agree on which is best.

open_questions.q: How can scientists tell exactly how fast one particle moves, when it is too small to see?
open_questions.why_open: They measure the effect of a huge number of particles, such as pressure. Following one single particle for long is much harder, and the methods are still improving.

open_questions.q: How do particles of a liquid cool into a glass instead of a crystal?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand the broad picture. They are still arguing about the exact way the particles stop moving as a runny liquid turns hard.
