maths.context: This is about the colour dilution test, with made-up numbers.
maths.problem: Pretend cup 1 holds 1,000,000 colour specks. Each spoonful carries one tenth of the specks forward to the next cup. How many specks are in cup 4? In which cup are there only 10 specks?
maths.answer: 1,000 specks in cup 4. Cup 6 has 10 specks.
maths.explain: Cup 2 has 1,000,000 divided by 10, which is 100,000. Cup 3 has 10,000. Cup 4 has 1,000. Cup 5 has 100. Cup 6 has 10. Each cup has one tenth of the one before. A real drop holds far more specks than a million.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by 10 again and again is a pattern. Spotting it lets you work out any cup without doing every step.

chart.title: Made-up colour specks in each cup

maths.context: This is about the squeeze test with a syringe full of air.
maths.problem: A syringe holds 10 millilitres of air. After a hard push, the plunger is at the 4 millilitre mark. By how many millilitres did the air squash? What fraction of the starting amount is that?
maths.answer: 6 millilitres. That is 6 tenths, or 3 fifths, of the start.
maths.explain: 10 take away 4 is 6. The air squashed by 6 out of 10 millilitres, which is the fraction 6/10. Both 6 and 10 divide by 2, so it is the same as 3/5.
maths.why_maths: Writing the squash as a fraction lets you compare squashes from syringes of different sizes.

maths.context: This is about the squeeze test again.
maths.problem: In the syringe test, the air squashed from 10 millilitres to 4 millilitres. What percentage of its starting size was the air squashed down to? Is the pressure now more than or less than double the starting pressure?
maths.answer: 40 percent. The pressure is more than double.
maths.explain: 4 out of 10 is 4/10, which is 40 out of 100, or 40 percent. The same particles are in 4 tenths of the space, so there are 10 divided by 4, or 2 and a half, times as many in each millilitre. That is more than double.
maths.why_maths: A percentage shows how much of the space is left, so that you can compare any squeeze.

maths.context: This is about the Full Jar activity.
maths.problem: A jug held 300 millilitres of chana. Then 85 millilitres of mustard seeds went in, and then 40 millilitres of water. How much stuff is now in the jug? How much is the total more than the 300 millilitres of chana?
maths.answer: 425 millilitres. That is 125 more than the chana alone.
maths.explain: 300 plus 85 is 385. 385 plus 40 is 425. The jug now holds 425 millilitres of stuff. The extra is 425 take away 300, which is 125 millilitres. The extra fitted into the gaps.
maths.why_maths: Adding the three amounts shows how much extra went into the gaps.

maths.context: This is about the three tries in the squeeze test.
maths.problem: Three tries with air in the syringe gave a squash of 4, 6 and 5 millilitres. What is the middle number? Why do scientists use the middle number and not just the first try?
maths.answer: 5 millilitres. It protects against one odd try.
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order: 4, 5, 6. The middle one is 5. A single try could be odd, for example if the seal leaked. The middle number is less affected by one odd result.
maths.why_maths: Using the middle number makes results fairer when each try is a little different.

maths.context: This is about the number of particles in a drop of water.
maths.problem: A drop of water holds about a thousand million million million water particles. How many zeros does that number have if you write it out? Write the first part: a thousand is 1,000.
maths.explain: A thousand has 3 zeros. A million has 6 zeros. Each 'million' adds 6 zeros, and there are three of them, so 3 plus 6 plus 6 plus 6 is 21 zeros. The number is 1 followed by 21 zeros.
maths.why_maths: Counting zeros is the way to compare huge numbers quickly.

maths.context: This is about a bicycle pump pushing air into a tyre.
maths.problem: A tyre holds 2,000 millilitres and starts full of outside air at normal pressure. Each pump stroke pushes in 500 millilitres more outside air. After 4 strokes, how many times as many air particles are in the tyre as at the start? So about how many times the outside pressure is it?
maths.answer: Twice as many. About twice the outside pressure.
maths.explain: 4 strokes of 500 is 2,000 millilitres of extra outside air. The tyre had 2,000 millilitres, so it now holds 2,000 plus 2,000 which is 4,000 millilitres of outside air squeezed into 2,000. That is twice as many particles in the same space, so about twice the pressure.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how much air goes in with the size of the tyre predicts the pressure.

maths.context: This is about how fast gas particles move.
maths.problem: Air particles fly at about 500 metres every second. If one could fly in a straight line, how far would it go in one minute? Give your answer in metres and in kilometres. A smell takes about five minutes to cross a 6 metre room. Why is this so much slower?
maths.answer: 30,000 metres, which is 30 kilometres. The smell zigzags.
maths.explain: 500 times 60 is 30,000 metres. 1,000 metres make a kilometre, so 30,000 metres is 30 kilometres. A smell particle is knocked in a new direction billions of times each second, so it zigzags and makes little progress.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a straight-line distance with the real distance shows how much the bumping slows the smell.

roots.context: We have squeezed air and water, and watched one drop of colour spread through cup after cup. Now we ask what it means that everything has a lot of room inside it, and what that says about us.

deep_truth.truth: In the syringe, the air squashed to under half its size, and the water hardly moved. Both are made of particles. The difference is the empty space between them. What looks like 'full' or 'nothing' is particles with less room or more room.
deep_truth.habit: We think a solid is full of stuff and a gas is nothing. That is wrong for the gas, because air is stuff too. It is also wrong for the solid, because it has gaps inside.
deep_truth.evidence: In the squeeze test, the air in the syringe squashed to about half, the water hardly moved, and the rice moved a little as the grains settled. In the jar test, the mustard seeds slid into the gaps between the dal and filled the jar. If your numbers differ, write them down as they are.

three.who_am_i: More than half of your weight is water. Your lungs fill with a gas, and the empty space between air particles is why you can breathe in and out.
three.what_is_life: A bee finds a flower by smell particles that drift through the air from far away. Many living beings find food, friends and danger by catching particles in the air or the water.
three.what_is_this_world: A rock, the sea, the air and the steam from a kettle are made of the same kinds of particles. They differ in how much room the particles have, and how fast they move.

roots.thread: Solid, liquid and gas are not three different kinds of stuff. They are three ways the same particles can behave, depending on how much room they have and how fast they move. Heating or cooling moves a substance from one way to another. A spoon and the steam from a kettle are not as far apart as they look.

teachings.source: Democritus of Abdera, as reported by Aristotle in the Metaphysics, Book 1
teachings.teaching: Democritus, an ancient Greek thinker, taught that everything is made of atoms and empty space. Atoms cannot be cut further. Different things come from different atoms joined in different ways.
teachings.link: Your syringe test showed the empty space. Air squashed because its particles moved into the room between them.

teachings.source: The Vaisheshika school, traditionally linked to the teacher Kanada
teachings.teaching: The Vaisheshika school of India taught that the world is made of tiny indivisible parts called paramanu, and that different things come from them joining in different ways. Scholars do not agree on the date, and some place its first ideas long before the common era.
teachings.link: Steel, water and steam are made of tiny parts joined and moving in different ways. That is the idea you tested with cups and syringes.

science.text: Gas pressure is made by particles hitting the walls of the container, and a hotter gas pushes harder.
Atoms are mostly empty space around a tiny nucleus, and the push of electrons between atoms is what makes a solid feel hard.
Physicists describe the smallest things as ripples in fields, not as tiny balls, and they do not agree on what, if anything, lies beneath.

other_view.view: The particle picture is a tool for predicting what happens, and we should not say that particles are real in the way a chair is real. A model is good if it predicts well. Whether the particles are really out there is a separate question that experiments may never settle.

practice.title: Three crowds in one breath
practice.say: Stand with your feet apart. First, be a solid. Hold your body stiff and shake only a little. Breathe in slowly. Now be a liquid. Sway and let your arms flow. Breathe out slowly. Now be a gas. Spread your arms wide and take up all the room you can. Notice how much space each one needed.

ask: If a solid, a liquid and a gas can be the same particles, what makes a spoon a spoon and steam steam?
Nobody can see the empty space in air. Is it real? How do you know?
Your hand cannot pass through a table, though both are mostly empty space. What does that tell you about what 'solid' means?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was checked against what is known to happen at home, but has not yet been run by a family. How Far Does One Drop Go uses six clear cups, a teaspoon and food colour. Each cup holds ten teaspoons in all, and each spoonful passed on is a tenth of the cup before, so the colour is one tenth, one hundredth and so on. Red and blue colours usually fade out between cup three and cup five. If your colour fades by cup two or three, use three drops in cup 1, and if cup 6 is still bright, add more cups. The Squeeze Test needs a plastic syringe with no needle, from a chemist. Air usually squashes to between 3 and 6 millilitres, and the plunger springs back. Water hardly moves, as long as every bubble is tapped out. A leaking seal is the most common problem, so the step shows how to test it. Full Jar uses food that should not be eaten afterwards. Rice Tray Crowds is a model, and the step says where it is wrong. Which Crowd is a card game with 24 cards that were written out in full. Facts to check: the claim that Waterston worked in Bombay, the number of particles in a drop of water (about 1.7 thousand million million million), and the speed of air particles.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells the story of how people found out that a gas is made of particles flying about, and why it took so long.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many scientists pictured a gas as particles sitting still, each pushing its neighbours away, like people in a crowd holding out their arms. This picture gave the right rule for squashing a gas, so most people accepted it. In 1738, a Swiss scientist named Daniel Bernoulli wrote that a gas is particles flying about and hitting the walls, and that this makes the pressure. Heat, he said, makes them fly faster. Almost nobody paid attention. In 1845, a Scottish scientist named John James Waterston, who was working in Bombay at the time, sent a paper on the same idea to the Royal Society in London. It was reportedly judged to be nonsense, and the paper lay unread in the archives. In the 1850s and 1860s, Rudolf Clausius and James Clerk Maxwell worked out the maths in full, and it matched measurements. Lord Rayleigh found Waterston's paper in the archives in 1891, and it was published in 1892.
how_we_found_out.who: Daniel Bernoulli, a Swiss scientist, and John James Waterston, a Scottish scientist, followed by Rudolf Clausius and James Clerk Maxwell
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought the particles of a gas sit in fixed places and push each other away. The flying-particle picture explains why heat raises the pressure and why gases spread into each other, which the fixed-place picture cannot.
